common_name: Sapphire Skies Yucca (Patented Silver-Blue Beaked Yucca)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil so roots establish before winter; raise the planting site or amend heavily with coarse grit in any soil that holds moisture.

directions: Sapphire Skies is a selected, patented clone of beaked yucca chosen for exceptionally intense silvery-blue foliage color and a tighter, more symmetrical rosette than seed-grown plants of the species. It shares the parent species' slow single-trunk habit, eventually lifting its dense, globe-shaped head of rigid, narrow leaves several feet into the air, and tolerates cold surprisingly well for a Chihuahuan Desert native given excellent drainage. Grow it in full sun in lean, rocky or sandy soil, and never in a low spot where winter moisture can collect around the crown, since rot rather than cold is the real threat to this plant. Because it is a named clonal selection, propagate only by removing rooted basal offsets rather than by seed, which will not come true.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; this species is less cold-tolerant than its close relative Yucca rostrata and appreciates a warm, sheltered position outside the mildest zones.

directions: Native to limestone slopes in Nuevo Leon, Mexico, linearleaf yucca is a close relative of beaked yucca but carries thinner, more numerous, grass-like blue-green leaves with fewer of the curling marginal fibers typical of that species, giving its rounded head a finer, softer texture. Over many years it develops a slender, usually solitary trunk topped by a dense, nearly spherical crown of foliage, making it a striking accent for rock gardens and dry courtyards where its refined silhouette can be appreciated up close. It demands the same razor-sharp drainage as other tree yuccas and is more cold-sensitive than Yucca rostrata, so it performs best in warm, arid climates or as a large container specimen moved under cover where winters are wet and cold. Remove basal offsets to propagate true divisions, since seedlings are slow and variable.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this coastal-native selection tolerates salt spray and sandy soil better than most variegated architectural perennials.

directions: Variegata is a striking sport of the coastal Spanish dagger, its stiff, upright, sword-shaped leaves broadly edged in creamy white to pale yellow around a blue-green center, giving the clumping, short-trunked rosette strong color even before the tall summer flower spike of nodding, white, often purple-tinged bells appears. Like the species it is native to dunes and sandy shores of the southeastern coastal plain, so it shrugs off salt spray, wind, and poor sandy soil that would trouble most other variegated perennials, making it a standout for seaside and xeriscape plantings alike. Give it full sun for the best leaf color and contrast, since shaded plants revert to weaker variegation and a looser habit, and provide sharp drainage to avoid crown rot in heavy soils. Propagate only from rooted basal offsets, since seed-grown plants will not reliably retain the variegated pattern.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in lean, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; this high-elevation Colorado Plateau native is among the most cold-hardy of all yuccas and needs no winter protection.

directions: Harriman's yucca is a diminutive, stemless species of the Colorado Plateau and Four Corners region, forming a tight low rosette of narrow, blue-green leaves edged with curling white fibers, rarely more than a foot across even at maturity. In late spring a modest but showy flower stalk rises a foot or two above the foliage, carrying pendulous, creamy-white bells that make an outsized display relative to the plant's small stature. Its high-desert origin makes it exceptionally cold-hardy and an excellent choice for rock gardens, gravel beds, and xeriscapes in colder climates where larger tree-form yuccas cannot survive, provided drainage is sharp and winter soil moisture is minimal. Propagate by separating offsets that form slowly at the base of established clumps, since named material and regional ecotypes vary in leaf width and cold tolerance.
